title: The Oregon Trail
traveller: The emigrants of the Great Migration of 1843
intro: The Oregon Trail was a wagon route of 2,170 miles (3,490 km) from the Missouri River to valleys in Oregon Territory. In the Great Migration of 1843, an estimated 700 to 1,000 emigrants set out for Oregon, led at first by John Gantt, and later by Marcus Whitman.
ending: Nearly all the settlers of the 1843 wagon trains reached the Willamette Valley by early October, and a passable wagon trail now existed from the Missouri River to The Dalles. The Barlow Road, completed in 1846, made the whole way passable for wagons.

legs.title: From the Missouri to South Pass

stops.text: Independence was the main jumping off point, the common head of the Santa Fe Trail and the Oregon Trail. Travellers had to ferry across the Missouri River, then followed the Santa Fe Trail to near present-day Topeka, Kansas.
stops.quote: Travelers starting in Independence had to ferry across the Missouri River.

stops.text: The army fort, established in 1848, lay about 200 miles (320 km) from the Missouri River. Nearly all the trail's offshoots converged near it along the Platte, and it was the first place to buy supplies, make repairs, get medical aid or mail a letter.
stops.quote: The army-maintained fort was the first chance on the trail to buy emergency supplies, do repairs, get medical aid, or mail a letter.

stops.text: Travellers on the Platte passed landmarks in Nebraska including Courthouse and Jail Rocks, Chimney Rock and Scotts Bluff. Until about 1870 hundreds of thousands of bison migrated through Nebraska, and most travellers killed several for fresh meat.
stops.quote: Notable landmarks in Nebraska include Courthouse and Jail Rocks, Chimney Rock, Scotts Bluff, and Ash Hollow State Historical Park.

stops.text: Fort Laramie was a former fur trading outpost, first named Fort John, bought by the U.S. Army in 1848 to protect travellers on the trails. Most cholera outbreaks on the Platte ended here.
stops.quote: Fort Laramie, at the junction of the Laramie River and the North Platte River, was a major stopping point.

stops.text: Where the North Platte veered south, the trail crossed it to the Sweetwater River valley, which heads almost due west. Independence Rock stands on the Sweetwater, which had to be crossed up to nine times.
stops.quote: Independence Rock is located on the Sweetwater River.

stops.text: The trail crossed the Continental Divide at South Pass. It then ran southwest over Big Sandy Creek to the Green River, a dangerous crossing at high water in July and August, where three to five ferries worked at peak times.
stops.quote: The Sweetwater would have to be crossed up to nine times before the trail crosses over the Continental Divide at South Pass, Wyoming.

legs.title: From Fort Bridger to Fort Boise

stops.text: Beyond the Green River the main trail met the Blacks Fork and Fort Bridger. In 1847 Brigham Young and the Mormon pioneers left the trail here for Utah, while the main trail veered northwest to the Bear River valley.
stops.quote: From Fort Bridger, the main trail, comprising several variants, veered northwest over the Bear River Divide and descended to the Bear River Valley.

stops.text: The trail followed the Bear River northwest to Soda Springs, a favourite attraction of the pioneers, who marvelled at the hot carbonated water. West of it the main trail turned northwest along the Portneuf River valley.
stops.quote: Many stopped and did their laundry in the hot water as there was usually plenty of good grass and fresh water available.

stops.text: Fort Hall was an old fur trading post on the Snake River, founded by Nathaniel Jarvis Wyeth and company and sold in 1837 to the Hudson's Bay Company. Nearly all travellers were given some aid and supplies there if available.
stops.quote: Fort Hall was an old fur trading post located on the Snake River.

stops.text: Near present-day Glenns Ferry, most emigrants crossed the swift Snake River here by ferry, or by driving or floating wagons and swimming teams. Hidden holes in the bed made it treacherous, and before ferries there were several drownings nearly every year.
stops.quote: Here most emigrants used the divisions of the river caused by three islands to cross the difficult and swift Snake River by ferry or by driving or sometimes floating their wagons and swimming their teams across.

stops.text: The north side of the Snake had better water and grass, and the Boise River valley was a welcome relief. The last Snake crossing, near Old Fort Boise, was made on bull boats, and young Native American boys were often hired to drive and ride the stock across.
stops.quote: The next crossing of the Snake River was near Old Fort Boise.

legs.title: From the Blue Mountains to Oregon City

stops.text: Across what became Oregon the trail passed the Malheur River, Farewell Bend and the Burnt River canyon to the La Grande valley, below the Blue Mountains. In 1843 settlers cut a wagon road over them, passable to wagons for the first time.
stops.quote: The trail then went to the Malheur River and then past Farewell Bend on the Snake River, up the Burnt River canyon and northwest to the La Grande valley before coming to the Blue Mountains.

stops.text: The trail went to the Whitman Mission near Fort Nez Perce in Washington. There some travellers built rafts or hired boats for the Columbia, while others went on by wagon. After 1847 the trail bypassed the closed mission.
stops.quote: The trail went to the Whitman Mission near Fort Nez Perce in Washington until 1847 when the Whitmans were killed by Native Americans.

stops.text: At the Columbia, stopped by the Cascade Mountains and Mount Hood, some gave up their wagons or floated them downriver on boats or rafts. Livestock were driven around Mount Hood, and the Barlow Road, a toll road, was cut from here in 1846.
stops.quote: Arriving at the Columbia at The Dalles and stopped by the Cascade Mountains and Mount Hood, some gave up their wagons or disassembled them and put them on boats or rafts for a trip down the Columbia River.

stops.text: Travellers on the Columbia made a portage of 1.6 miles (2.6 km) around the Cascade Rapids before reaching the Willamette River near Oregon City, the trail's nominal end. Many settlers branched off or stopped short of it.
stops.quote: The Oregon Trail's nominal termination point was Oregon City, at the time the proposed capital of the Oregon Territory.

notes: Revised from the held draft with the second article (Route of the Oregon Trail). The route is a network used by many parties over decades, so no stop carries a date; founding years and the like stand in the texts. Fort Hall's founding is given as 1832 and as 1834 in the route article: the text names no year. The 1843 road over the Blue Mountains is in the text of the La Grande valley stop (date null: it is a road over the range, not a dated event at the town). Left out: Kansas crossings and Ash Hollow (no stop with its own event that fits a place with a point), the Green River (a river), Salmon Falls (a fishing place, little else), the Sublette-Greenwood Cutoff, Lander Road and other cutoffs (not the main trail). The route article names no Native nation along the trail except Sauk in Iowa, which is off the trail; it says only 'Native Americans' and 'Indians'. The by-field of every stop is land although many travelled down the Columbia by boat.
